quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Risk and Identity
quizzes.intro: CIA, risk language, authentication, and passwords.

options.text: Cookies, Internet, Apps
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
Coding, Installation, Automation
Compliance, Invoices, Audits only

questions.explanation: CIA organizes classic security goals: secrecy, trustworthiness of data, and reliable access.

wrongExplanations.a: Unrelated expansion of the acronym. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Those words are not the CIA triad. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Compliance matters but is not what CIA expands to.

questions.prompt: A vulnerability is best described as:

options.text: A guaranteed breach that already happened
A weakness that a threat could exploit
Any security tool you bought
A backup success report

questions.explanation: Vulnerabilities are weaknesses; risk appears when threats can exploit them against assets.

wrongExplanations.a: An exploited incident is an event/impact, not the definition of vulnerability.
wrongExplanations.c: Tools are controls, not vulnerabilities. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Backups are controls/recovery assets. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Authentication differs from authorization because authentication:

options.text: Grants every permission automatically
Verifies identity, while authorization decides allowed actions
Deletes logs
Is identical to encryption

questions.explanation: AuthN answers who you are; AuthZ answers what you may do.

wrongExplanations.a: Identity proof is not automatic full access. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Logging is separate. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Encryption protects data, not identity decisions. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

options.text: Plain text in a spreadsheet
Slow salted hashes designed for passwords
Reversible encryption with one shared key in the app UI
Browser localStorage for every user

questions.explanation: Password hashing with salt/work factor lets systems verify secrets without storing them directly.

wrongExplanations.a: Plain text is catastrophic if leaked. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Reversible storage is weaker for password verification use cases.
wrongExplanations.d: Frontend storage is not a password database. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

options.text: It makes passwords unnecessary forever in all systems
Stolen passwords alone are often not enough to break in
It replaces backups
It removes the need for patching

questions.explanation: An extra factor raises attacker cost after credential theft.

wrongExplanations.a: Passwords often still exist alongside MFA. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Backups remain necessary. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Patching remains necessary. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Attacks and Defenses
quizzes.intro: Phishing, web risks, encryption, and least privilege.

questions.prompt: A strong phishing warning sign is:

options.text: A calm expected receipt from a known vendor with no ask
Urgent pressure to click a strange link and enter credentials
A password manager autofill on a site you intentionally opened
HTTPS on a trusted bank domain you typed yourself

questions.explanation: Urgency plus unexpected credential requests are classic social-engineering tells.

wrongExplanations.a: Expected receipts are normal. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Autofill on intentional visits is not phishing by itself.
wrongExplanations.d: Typed trusted HTTPS destinations are good practice. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: SQL injection risk is reduced by:

options.text: Trusting all client input
Parameterized queries / safe DB access patterns and server-side checks
Disabling HTTPS
Showing detailed DB errors to strangers

questions.explanation: Safe query construction and validation stop hostile input from becoming executable SQL.

wrongExplanations.a: Client input is hostile by default. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: HTTPS does not replace injection defenses. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Verbose errors help attackers. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

options.text: Faster CSS rendering
Confidentiality of data at rest or in transit when keys are protected
Automatic perfect authorization
Deleting the need for MFA

questions.explanation: Encryption protects secrecy; authorization and identity controls remain separate.

wrongExplanations.a: Encryption is unrelated to CSS. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Encrypted data can still be accessed by authorized app paths.
wrongExplanations.d: MFA remains useful. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Least privilege reduces damage after compromise because:

options.text: Attackers gain admin everywhere by default
The stolen account can access only what it needed for its job
Logs are turned off
Patches become unnecessary

questions.explanation: Narrow permissions limit how far an attacker can move with one account.

wrongExplanations.a: That outcome is what least privilege prevents. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Logging should increase, not stop. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Patching remains required. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: A publicly exposed storage bucket with private files should first be:

options.text: Ignored until next quarter
Restricted immediately while preserving evidence and starting incident response
Shared more widely for convenience
Used as a marketing CDN without review

questions.explanation: Contain exposure fast, then investigate and notify as needed.

wrongExplanations.a: Delay worsens impact. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Wider sharing increases harm. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Sensitive private files are not casual CDN fodder.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Security Judgment
quizzes.intro: Apply risk thinking across people, process, and technology.

options.text: One magic tool replaces all other controls
Overlapping controls so one failure does not cause total loss
Never monitoring systems
Avoiding backups because encryption exists

questions.explanation: Layered controls raise attacker cost and reduce blast radius.

wrongExplanations.a: No single tool is enough. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Monitoring is part of depth. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Backups remain critical. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: After a suspected account takeover, a sensible early response is:

options.text: Post the password in chat for teammates
Force logout/disable access, rotate credentials, preserve logs, communicate carefully
Delete all logs to reduce embarrassment
Disable MFA across the company

questions.explanation: Containment, credential hygiene, evidence, and communication are core IR moves.

wrongExplanations.a: Sharing passwords spreads compromise. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Logs are evidence. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Disabling MFA worsens security. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

options.text: Scanning any website that looks interesting
Authorization and legal scope before testing systems you do not own
Publishing customer data to prove a point
Skipping incident documentation

questions.explanation: Permission and scope separate professional testing from illegal access.

wrongExplanations.a: Curiosity without permission is not authorization. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Publishing private data is unethical/illegal. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Documentation supports learning and compliance. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Email accounts deserve special protection because:

options.text: They are never used for recovery
They often reset many other accounts if compromised
They cannot use MFA
They replace password managers

questions.explanation: Mailbox takeover frequently cascades into other services via recovery flows.

wrongExplanations.a: Email is commonly used for recovery. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Email can and should use MFA. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Password managers remain essential. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

options.text: Buying tools without process or ownership
Managing risk to assets with controls, monitoring, and response habits
Assuming breaches are impossible if you use HTTPS
Ignoring insider mistakes and accidents

questions.explanation: Security is ongoing risk management across people, process, and technology.

wrongExplanations.a: Tools without process fail. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: HTTPS helps but is not total safety. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Accidents and insiders matter. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
